extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers preparing mathematical texts (undergraduate/graduate mathematicians, authors of proofs and papers)
extracted.subtask_description: A concise style guide for writing mathematics covering notation, equations, punctuation, grammar, definitions, theorem/proof structure, fonts, and LaTeX tips to make mathematical exposition clear and correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin sentences with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting a sentence with a mathematical symbol; introduce the object in words first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "√2 is irrational." Good: "The number √2 is irrational." Use words to start sentences; similarly, avoid sentences that begin with variables without words. Examples show rephrasing with "The number", "Let n be an even number. Thus n = 2m...", or "In this case, f(x) is periodic."

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place unrelated symbols adjacent without words or punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: If two symbols are not part of the same mathematical expression, separate them with words or grammatical marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "If n≠0 n^2>0." Good: "If n≠0 then n^2>0." Also: write "x_k for 1 ≤ k ≤ n" or "x_k where 1 ≤ k ≤ n" rather than putting the range immediately adjacent to the symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation that fits the context
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing notation, pick symbols that make sense in context (common sense naming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Let m be a prime." Good: "Let p be a prime." Use letters typically associated with the object (e.g., p for prime, x for element) to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always define new notation and state its type
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly define any new notation and specify whether it is a number, function, set element, etc., and its logical standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very bad: "Since n is composite, n = ab." Better: "Since n is composite, n = ab for some integers a and b greater than 1." Also clarify quantification (e.g., `f(n) ∈ Z for every n ∈ Z`).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give multiple meanings to a variable in a single argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reusing the same variable name for different objects within the same proof or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example uses m for both even integers leading to logical error. Use distinct names (a = 2m, b = 2n) and state the existence of separate integers m and n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading meaning into notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pack several pieces of meaning into one shorthand symbol; be explicit about properties and types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Let x > 0 ∈ Z." Good: "Let x be a positive integer." Or: "Let x be an integer, with x > 0."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard set symbols correctly (Z, Q, R, C denote sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat Z, Q, R, C as sets, not as individual numbers; avoid writing 'Let C be a complex number.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Let C be a complex number." Good: "Let z be a complex number." Or: "Choose z ∈ C."

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use logical symbols (∀, ∃, ∧, ∨) in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out logical quantifiers and connectives in words in normal mathematical writing (except in logic papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "a = 0 ∧ b = 1." Good: "a = 0 and b = 1." Bad: "If ∃ a root..." Good: "If there is a root..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'for all' (∀) correctly — it means 'for all/for every', not 'all/every' alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful translating ∀ into English; use grammatical phrasing like 'All ...' or 'Every ...' where appropriate but remember ∀ has quantificational meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of misuse: "∀ square matrices with nonzero determinant are invertible." Correct: "All square matrices with nonzero determinant are invertible." Also: do not write "... agree at ∀ points"; write "... agree at all points."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid informal or blackboard abbreviations (WLOG, s.t., iﬀ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out phrases such as 'without loss of generality', 'such that', and 'if and only if' in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "WLOG, we can assume x > 0." Good: "Without loss of generality, we can assume x > 0." Bad: "x s.t. f(x) > 0" → Good: "x such that f(x) > 0."

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit superfluous notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a piece of notation is not used again or serves no purpose, do not introduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "Every differentiable function f is continuous." (superfluous f) Good: "Every differentiable function is continuous." Use notation only when referenced later (e.g., A and det A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish equation vs expression
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation has the form A = B; an expression is a mathematical formula without an equality sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: x^2 − 3x + 4 is an expression, not an equation. Use correct terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important equations and label those you will refer to later
rubrics_metrics.description: Place important equations on their own lines and number them if you will reference them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to refer back later use labels like (2.1). If only referring immediately before/after, a label may be omitted but displaying helps the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stack multi-step computations for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a computation has multiple steps (especially more than two), present it in stacked (multi-line) form rather than inline chaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: chaining many equals signs in one line. Good: break into separate lines, possibly aligning equals signs, and use indentation/punctuation so each step is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed equations as part of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat displayed equations as part of the surrounding sentence and punctuate with periods, commas, or nothing as grammar dictates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an equation ends a sentence, put a period after the displayed line. If it occurs mid-sentence, use a comma if a pause naturally occurs. Examples show different acceptable punctuations and placing of commas/periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant parentheses in mathematical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use parentheses that serve no purpose as they clutter expressions and text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: (x+y)(x−y) = (x^2 − y^2) — parentheses around x^2 − y^2 are unnecessary. Similarly drop parentheses in textual phrases like 'product (a1a2 · · · an)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parentheses to disambiguate subtraction vs negative sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert parentheses when necessary to make the intended grouping and signs clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very bad: (a + b) − c = −ac − bc (ambiguous). Better: (a + b)(−c) = −ac − bc or (a + b) · (−c) = −ac − bc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas appropriately; avoid misplaced commas and run-ons
rubrics_metrics.description: Place commas where natural pauses occur; avoid comma splices and where a period or no punctuation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "The condition we want is, a = 2b." Good: "The condition we want is a = 2b." For run-ons, prefer a period or subordinating conjunction: "The set is infinite. We pick..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Let..., then...' comma construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect 'Let...' and subsequent clause with a comma; instead use a period or a conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very bad: "Let n be an even number, then n = 2m..." Good: "Let n be an even number. Then n = 2m..." or "Let n be an even number, so n = 2m..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader where you are going (signpost arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit statements to indicate the proof method, structure, or strategy before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: "We will prove this by induction on n." "We argue by contradiction." "Now we consider the converse direction." Such signposting orients the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use key words to show reasoning and vary phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ connective words (since, because, on the other hand, observe, note) to expose the structure of reasoning and avoid monotonous repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider rewriting paragraphs to avoid repetitive short sentences; the handout gives an example improving a repeated 'Then' sequence into a concise chained explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate ordinary sentences and use apostrophes correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard punctuation rules in prose, and use "it's" only for "it is" and "its" for possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "It’s clear that f(x) has a real root since it’s degree is odd." Correct forms given. If unsure, rephrase to avoid pitfalls: "Since f(x) has odd degree, clearly it has a real root."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentence fragments and run-on sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Write complete sentences and split or combine clauses appropriately to avoid fragments and comma splices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad fragment: "How to describe rotations in R^3." Good: "We will explain how to describe rotations in R^3." Bad run-on: split into two sentences or use relative clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep verb tenses consistent; state mathematical facts in present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent tenses; mathematical truths are timeless and should typically be stated in the present tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "In 1873, Hermite proved that e was transcendental." Good: "In 1873, Hermite proved that e is transcendental." Also: avoid mixing past/present improperly in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure subject-verb agreement and correct singular/plural usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Match verbs to their subjects correctly; treat collective nouns appropriately in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "The set of real numbers are uncountable." Good: "The set of real numbers is uncountable." But "The real numbers are uncountable." is correct when the real numbers are the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch spelling and idiom; prefer single-word forms where conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell mathematical and common words correctly and use conventional single-word forms (e.g., 'counterexample', 'straightforward').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-native speakers should be cautious about transferring grammatical rules from their own language. Look up uncertain words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary repetition within sentences and paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat long words or definitions unnecessarily; once defined, do not restate the same definition each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: repeating explanations; Good: concise references. Example: after defining π, don't restate the definition each time π is mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to paragraph boundaries and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Place sentences and examples so that paragraphs form coherent blocks; don't end a paragraph with a statement and start the next only to explain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move transitional phrases (e.g., "For example,") to the logical place where the example begins rather than at paragraph breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure parallel items in the same grammatical form to aid clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: mixing forms in parallel lists. Good: "decomposed into algebraic and transcendental numbers" rather than repeating 'numbers' irregularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid informal language in formal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace colloquial or hyperbolic words with measured academic phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "It is mind-boggling..." Good: "It is surprising..." or "It is striking..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the roles of theorem, lemma, and corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use names to indicate importance: theorem = main result, lemma = helper result used to prove a theorem, corollary = consequence of a theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order typically appears as Lemma, Theorem, Corollary. A lemma should generally precede the theorem it supports; a corollary follows its theorem. There is no necessity of lemmas or corollaries but misuse can confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization and reference conventions for numbered results and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitalization for numbered items and plain words for non-numbered references (e.g., 'by Theorem 2.1' but 'by the previous theorem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, write 'in Section 2' but 'the next section'. Use 'Lemma 6.3' vs 'the next lemma' appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format proofs: start with 'Proof' and end with a QED symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs with the label 'Proof' and terminate them with an ending symbol such as a square or tombstone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to place a short proof (e.g., proof that √2 is irrational) use a proper proof environment after the statement being proved; do not mix proof text into theorem statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not put part of a proof inside the statement of a theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem statements should state results only; proofs and proof hints belong in a separate proof environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: "Theorem. √2 is irrational, and it can be proved by contradiction." Instead, state the theorem alone and follow with the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: present the term being defined clearly and separately
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition describes a new word; put the term being defined in italics or bold and avoid embedding properties or examples inside the definition environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place theorems or results inside a definition. Properties (closure under addition) should appear after the definition as propositions/theorems. Examples belong after the definition environment, not inside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make a definition into a theorem or vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure definitions are descriptive (what the word means) and not statements requiring proof; conversely, do not bury definitional content inside a theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad definition: giving a property that requires proof (e.g., closure under addition) as part of the definition. Keep definitions minimal and factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate fonts: single-letter variables italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-letter mathematical variables and single-letter function names should be set in italics (math mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Let p be a prime' with p italic. When typesetting in LaTeX, math mode will italicize these automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers are never in italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set numerals in italic font in mathematical text or formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write x^2 − 3x + 1 (not with italic numerals). Avoid using italic numbers anywhere; some may disagree but the handout strongly advises against italic numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display theorem/lemma/corollary statements in italic via environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proper theorem-like environments that italicize statements rather than forcing italics manually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In LaTeX, use the theorem/lemma/corollary environments rather than switching fonts directly to achieve the conventional italic styling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write multi-letter standard function names in upright (non-italic) font
rubrics_metrics.description: Function names like sin, cos, log should appear in upright font, not in italic like single-letter variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In LaTeX use the standard function commands (\sin, \log, etc.) which format such names upright even in theorem environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting: definitions and examples should not be italicized except the term
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put the text of definitions and examples in italics; only the term being defined should be emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics/bold solely for the term; body text of the definition/example remains upright to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conventional notation for indexed sequences (e.g., Fibonacci numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard subscript/superscript formatting (e.g., F_n) rather than awkward inline versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout emphasizes proper typesetting of sequences like Fibonacci numbers as F_n (with subscript) rather than awkward concatenations that blur meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX tip: handle special URL characters correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: When typesetting URLs, be careful with characters like %, _, and ∼; consult tex.stackexchange for proper handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tilde can disappear if not treated correctly; search tex.stackexchange for existing answers to common URL-escaping problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX tip: produce left (opening) double quotes correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two left single quotes (``) to produce a left double quote in TeX/LaTeX rather than the straight-quote character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typing the usual double-quote key yields ”here" instead of “here”. Use ``here'' in LaTeX source.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX tip: indicate multiplication with · or juxtaposition, not 'x' or '*'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the centered dot (·) or simple juxtaposition for multiplication in typeset mathematics; avoid using the letter 'x' or the asterisk '*' as multiplication symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: x · y or xy are preferred; × may be used in limited contexts but not lowercase x or *.
